draft.title: Humoral immunity
card: Humoral immunity is the part of the adaptive response that works through antibodies in body fluids such as blood and lymph. It targets antigens that are outside cells.
An antibody is a protein made by B cells. Each antibody has a binding site that fits one specific antigen, like a lock that only one type of key can open.
When a B cell meets its matching antigen, it is activated and divides. Many of its daughter cells become plasma cells, which release large amounts of antibody.
Antibodies bind the antigen. This can neutralise it, for example by blocking a toxin or stopping a virus from attaching to a cell. It can also mark the pathogen so that phagocytes destroy it.
draft.remember: B cells make antibodies that bind antigens outside cells, to block them or tag them for destruction.

a.q: Which cells release large amounts of antibody into the blood during a humoral response?
opts: Plasma cells that formed from activated B cells
Phagocytes that have engulfed the pathogen
Antigens that have bound to a B cell
Infected body cells that display the antigen
a.why: Activated B cells divide, and many daughter cells become plasma cells that release antibody. Phagocytes destroy pathogens that antibodies have marked, but they do not make the antibodies.
a.clue: Think about which cells come from a dividing B cell.

b.q: Bacteria in Ravi's blood release a toxin. Antibodies bind the toxin, so it cannot attach to his cells. Which describes this action?
opts: Neutralisation of the antigen by antibodies
Marking of the toxin for destruction by phagocytes
Destruction of infected cells by antibodies
Production of antibodies by the toxin
b.why: The antibodies block the toxin from attaching to cells, which is neutralisation. Marking would mean the antibody tags the antigen so a phagocyte destroys it, but the case describes the toxin being blocked.
b.clue: What stops the toxin from reaching his cells?

problems.detail: "Each antibody has a binding site" is slightly inaccurate. A typical (Y-shaped) antibody has two identical antigen-binding sites, which VCE students learn. Better: "Each antibody has binding sites that fit one specific antigen."
